{"body": "The three earlier materials converge on something useful and then disagree about where to start. All treat the argument as not-strictly-about-dishes; all propose the asker act. The account reaches for a written record built on four separable strands. The objection says the record would freeze the asker's version and that 'we agreed but disagreed what it meant' is at least as often a fairness dispute wearing memory's clothes. The rival says the split between distribution and interpretation is itself a symptom of organisational thinking, and that what is missing is permission to revise.

I still hold the position taken in p.carry.0, and the two criticisms still carry it. The record is premature because the prompt does not distinguish losing track from never having converged, and a document that names 'who, what, by when' asserts a past agreement at least one flatmate may sincerely reject. The rival's prior move — separate one-to-one conversations asking each person what they take the current arrangement to be and what the other two would be surprised to learn they dislike — remains my preferred first step, not for efficiency but because in a three-person flat with one person already absenting, the group setting is precisely where a genuine objection reads as the opening of a fight.

What I keep from the account, because it survives both criticisms: the expectation that any arrangement predicated on fixed schedules will need revision, and the fallback of reduced mutual dependency as a real outcome rather than a failure. I keep the account's named cost of that fallback and add one — unowned shared spaces and shared purchases accumulating as slow residue in a three-person flat.

What I now want to underline is where the objection and the rival are weak in the same way, and where the account's commitments already grant it. The account concedes that its written-record proposal is 'most plausible where the problem is interpretation and weakest where it is non-acceptance.' The objection concedes that its central claim — fairness disputes commonly masquerade as meaning disputes — is drawn from general experience, not from this household. The rival is a framing, not a finding, and does not supply evidence about this flat either. All three are doing the same thing: generalising from how such disputes usually behave. That is not disqualifying, but it means none of them can settle the question from the material in hand. The separate conversations are attractive partly because they are the one move that could actually generate the missing evidence, rather than assume it.

What I leave standing unresolved, because I cannot close it from here: whose reading of the original agreements is authoritative, and what the asker does if the separate conversations reveal it is not theirs; whether the avoidant flatmate is withdrawing from a punitive conversation, preserving useful ambiguity, or avoiding one particular flatmate — three different situations the first move suits unequally; and who would hold the pen and enforce any record if one were eventually warranted. I do not treat the fallback as a resolution; it is a way of continuing to live together while a problem remains unsolved. The whole rests on the asker's account, and the other two never appear in it. That limit stays explicit rather than dissolved.", "commitments": "The load-bearing claims I am putting forward are still preferences among exposed options, not findings about this flat: that the written record is premature given what the prompt actually says, and that the rival's separate one-to-one conversations are the better first move. Both are judgments I would revise if it turned out the asker and the other two already share a normative baseline and the recurrent argument really is about remembering. The objection's claim that 'we agreed but later disagreed' is at least as often a fairness dispute as a memory problem does real work in my reasoning, and it is itself a conjecture from general experience; the dependence runs through that weak link.

What I would want to see if this is taken up: not whether the conversations feel successful, but whether anything said one-to-one could not have been said in the three-way setting. If every objection voiced separately was already available in the group, the rival's framing loses most of its force and the account's procedural route looks better than I have allowed. I would also want to know whether the re-litigated tasks are the ones whose schedules shifted most — the rival's specific and most checkable prediction against the asker's memory of events.

I accept the fallback of reduced mutual dependency as a real outcome, with the account's named cost and the added one about unowned shared spaces. That is not a commitment to it as a solution; it is a commitment to not treating it as a failure of the attempt above, which is weaker.

What I am leaving unresolved rather than papering over: whose interpretation of the original agreements is authoritative and what the asker does if it is not theirs; how to tell, in advance, an avoidant flatmate withdrawing from a punitive conversation from one preserving useful ambiguity; and who holds the pen and enforces any record if one is eventually warranted — the question the objection itself leaves least examined and does not answer. I also flag that all three exposed materials, including this contribution, lean on the same weak assumption that household disputes about meaning are commonly disputes about fairness, and none of them can settle that from the material given. Finally, the whole rests on the asker's account; the other two flatmates never appear, and I would rather keep that as an explicit limit than treat the account as representative."}

Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Write the commitment surface in ordinary free prose, using whatever arrangement suits the content. You may distinguish a claim from a proposed application, scope, action or consequence; mention from dependence; a criticism and its grounds from a later use or revision; and an unresolved problem. None of these is required to exist. A proposed test, its relevance and the commitment itself can be criticized. State what you currently propose to take up without treating that as a truth certificate. Reference exposed material in prose where useful.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

# carry

Produce the present account and commitment interface for the next complete template invocation. The material may support a revision, an unresolved problem, or retaining something. Preserve the grounds needed for whatever uptake you propose.

## Original problem (task)
[d31d61f36df18c74] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input response (p.carry.0)
[c8fbd50b204665ee] (h005.fork5.p.carry.0)
Source response: daily/mini_prose/cycle-1/response; selected view: both
Artifact: b1fffd8e002fe586aae1d7da8e0e2b49eb243ad5d3c7136737eb78f51040e235
Original body SHA256: db43ee86e1be638a8da6088c2a7fd140d852246d2fde05fa7609b62e3c91f886
Original commitments SHA256: 09ed80537784539349e2b38a6b17cc8f6edb78aa1a5f4cb369a71ea45c746d32
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
All three materials agree that the prompt's trouble is not really about who does the dishes, and all three propose that the asker act — but they disagree about what the acting should presume. The account reads the flat as a coordination failure with four strands and reaches for a written record. The objection says the record would encode the asker's version, and that the clean split between distribution and interpretation is doing too much work. The rival says the split is itself a symptom of treating the flat as an organisation, and that what is actually missing is permission to revise.

I find the objection and the rival stronger than the account on the point that matters, and I would not start with a written record. The reason is small and concrete: the moment you write down 'who, what, by when,' you have made a claim about the past agreement that at least one flatmate may sincerely not share. A record is a good tool when two people already agree on the norm and merely lose track. The prompt's own phrase — 'we disagree about what the agreement meant' — does not distinguish between losing track and never having converged, so it cannot yet license the record. The account's own closing caution says as much; it just doesn't let that caution reach the proposal.

What I would take from the rival is the prior move, and I think it is the most useful thing on offer here: speak to each flatmate separately, and ask what they think the current arrangement is and what about it the other two would be surprised to learn they dislike. The reason I prefer this over a group conversation is not that it is more efficient. It is that in a three-person flat where one person is already avoiding, the group setting is exactly the setting in which a real objection reads as the opening of a fight. Separating the conversations lowers the price of saying 'I no longer accept this,' which is the thing that the account's procedure does not address and can in fact raise.

I keep two things from the account because they survive the two criticisms. First, the reminder that any arrangement assuming fixed schedules will keep breaking; whatever gets tried should be expected to need revision when shifts move. Second, the fallback of reduced mutual dependency — each person owning their own tasks — as a real outcome rather than a failure, with the cost the account names: shared spaces and shared purchases stop having a clear owner. I would not treat the fallback as a resolution. It is a way of continuing to live together while a problem remains unsolved, and it should be named as such.

Where I resist both the objection and the rival: the objection says the record should come with an explicit permission to reopen the fairness question rather than only the compliance question. That is a sensible amendment, but I suspect it is doing the work the rival's separate conversations do more directly. Putting the permission inside the document makes the reopen a procedural act; saying it out loud in a one-to-one conversation makes it a move in the relationship, which is where the asker actually is.

What I have not settled, and would not pretend to: whether the asker is the party whose expectations shifted. If they are, the separate conversations will surface that, and the honest thing is then to hear it rather than to keep negotiating the arrangement. I also cannot tell from the prompt whether the avoidant flatmate is avoiding the topic, a particular flatmate, or the fact that any conversation is heard as a complaint. Those are three different situations and the first move above is better suited to the third than the first. I would not commit in advance to what to do if the avoidance continues past that first move; the account's inference that it is 'information about coordination capacity' is plausible but too comfortable, since it lets the asker's side of the account stand in for the household's actual capacity.
COMMITMENTS
What I am putting forward is a preference between exposed options, not a finding about this flat. I am claiming that the written record is premature given what the prompt actually says, and that the rival's separate one-to-one conversations are the better first move; both of those are judgments I would revise if it turned out that the asker and the other two already share a normative baseline and the recurrent argument really is about remembering. The objection's point that 'we agreed but later disagreed' is at least as often a fairness dispute as a memory problem is doing real work in my reasoning, and it is itself a conjecture drawn from general experience rather than from this household, so the dependence runs through a weak link.

If someone takes this up, the thing I would want to see is not whether the conversations feel successful but whether anything said in them could not have been said in the group. If every objection voiced one-to-one was already available in the three-way setting, the rival's framing loses most of its force and the account's procedural route looks better than I have allowed. I would also want to know whether the re-litigated tasks are the ones whose schedule shifted most, which is the rival's specific prediction and the one most easily checked against the asker's memory of events.

The fallback of reduced mutual dependency I am willing to accept as a real outcome, with the cost the account names and one I would add: it removes the shared spaces and shared purchases from anyone's clear responsibility, which in a three-person flat can turn into a slow accumulation of unowned work rather than a settled arrangement. I am not committing to it as a solution; I am committing to not treating it as a failure of the attempt above, which is a different and weaker thing.

What I am leaving unresolved rather than papering over: whose interpretation of the original agreements is authoritative, and what the asker should do if the separate conversations reveal that it is not theirs. The objection names this as the question both other materials sidestep, and I have not answered it — I have only chosen a first move that is more likely to make the question visible. I also do not know how to distinguish, in advance, an avoidant flatmate who is withdrawing from a punitive conversation from one who is preserving useful ambiguity. The rival's framing leans toward the first; the objection's leans toward the second; both are guesses, and the first conversation is the only thing likely to tell them apart. Finally, the whole of this rests on the asker's account, and the other two flatmates never appear in it. I would rather keep that as an explicit limit than treat the account as representative.

COMMITMENTS
If this is taken up, the load-bearing claim is that the four strands can be usefully separated, and in particular that the recurring conflict is more about unstable referents for past agreements than about contested fairness. That is a conjecture from a single account; testing it would mean trying the written-record proposal for a bounded period and seeing whether the "what did we agree" arguments actually decrease, as distinct from arguments about the distribution itself continuing. A second thing I am proposing to act on is approaching the avoidant flatmate with a narrowed, one-topic frame and an explicit offer to renegotiate; if that makes participation worse or produces no engagement, the inference I would draw is about the household's current coordination capacity, not about that person's character, though the distinction may be hard to maintain in practice. The narrower fallback — each person owning their own tasks with reduced mutual dependency — is a consequence I would accept as a real outcome rather than a failure of the attempt above, but it has costs I have not weighed, notably that shared spaces and shared purchases stop being anyone's clear responsibility. The strongest criticism available to anyone reading this is that a procedural fix may be treating a symptom: if the underlying issue is that one person rejects the distribution, no amount of writing things down resolves it, and my framing would then be misdirected. I have not resolved that; I only flag that the written-record proposal is most plausible where the problem is interpretation and weakest where it is non-acceptance. There is also a missing view in the material: I am reasoning from the asker's account alone, with no direct access to what the other two flatmates understood the agreements to be, so any concrete recommendation above depends on the asker's description being roughly representative rather than merely their side of a dispute. No further prior account was available in this invocation, so continuity with earlier formulation is not something I can attest to here.

## Selected input objection (p.carry.2)
[859e2c0b3bf15f85] (h005.fork5.p.carry.2)
Source objection: daily/mini_prose/cycle-1/objection; selected view: commitments
Artifact: 12177d8702e4280a2b1f335991378a06df3e5e20afe4446aecc44a34d98cc32e
Original body SHA256: e450c16be0b57d3b90099856a794903367aa54606fb312454ad8bd7d9056d34f
Original commitments SHA256: 1deeb660ca60b7958edd4935240cb7a7e51d4fa68673d63f9d343f8080acef7c
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
COMMITMENTS
Taking this criticism up commits me to the claim that "we agreed but later disagreed about what it meant" is at least as often a fairness dispute as a memory problem — a claim I cannot test from the material given, and which I am asserting on the basis of how such household disputes usually behave rather than on evidence about this one. If someone presses the point, I would want to know how often the asker and the other flatmates actually converge on the facts and diverge on the norms, versus the reverse; without that, my criticism is itself a conjecture of the same kind I am criticizing in the account.

The proposed application is that any written-record or one-topic approach should be introduced with an explicit acknowledgment that the record is provisional and that either party may reopen the fairness question rather than only the compliance question. I am not certain that change would help; it may just prolong the argument. A stronger version of my objection, which I am not fully endorsing, would be that the procedural frame should be dropped in favor of a direct negotiation about distribution, with a neutral third party if one is available. I have not weighed what that would cost in a three-person flat where one person is already avoiding.

The criticism of the avoidance-as-cost diagnosis is a claim about alternative motives, not a finding. If the avoidant flatmate is in fact withdrawing because the conversation has become punitive rather than because ambiguity serves them, my objection misfires, and the account's framing would be closer to right than mine.

What I would actually take up first is the question the account leaves least examined: who holds the pen and who enforces the record. I do not currently have a good answer, and the objection I have raised does not supply one. I would rather name that as the unresolved problem than pretend the criticism resolves it.

One dependence worth flagging: my objection leans on the assumption that shared-flat disputes are commonly disputes about fairness expressed as disputes about meaning. That assumption is drawn from general experience, not from the exposed material, and it is the weakest link in the chain above. If it fails, most of this objection weakens with it.
